---
title: "PK Model Selection: Submission Format Example"
subtitle: "Illustrative data and task definitions for contributors"
---

## Status and purpose

This example shows how to organize a benchmark submission. The CSV files contain one subject in each split and three concentration observations per subject. They are small illustrative snippets, not a complete dataset for evaluating modeling methods. No scientific validation or DOI is claimed for this example.

Use the [submission guide](../../submission-guide.qmd) and [benchmark template](https://github.com/AIML-SIG/pmx_benchmarks/blob/main/BENCHMARK_TEMPLATE.md) to prepare a complete submission.

**Goal:** 1 — Generic Benchmark ([Scope & Eligibility](../../scope.qmd)).

## Abstract

The example uses a pharmacokinetic model-selection question to illustrate the required files: documentation, metadata, training and test data, and a YAML data dictionary. The intended tasks are structural model selection, covariate selection, and concentration prediction. The snippets alone cannot support these tasks; a full submission would supply sufficient data and a reproducible generative process.

## Motivation

A useful model-selection benchmark could compare methods against a known generating model using the same tasks and evaluation criteria. For example, a synthetic case could specify a two-compartment model, weight effects on clearance and central volume, and covariates with no true effects.

A contributor would need to explain which existing datasets are most similar and how the new case adds value. This format example demonstrates the questions to address; it does not establish novelty or provide evidence for a particular generating model.

## Background

Structural and covariate selection are common pharmacometric modeling decisions. A complete synthetic benchmark would document the true model, parameter values, variability, dosing and sampling schedules, and the simulation code or procedure needed to reproduce the data. No such generation code is included here, so the values in the snippets should not be treated as validated simulations of a two-compartment model.

## Dataset description

The supplied files are:

| Split | Subject ID | Subjects | Dose rows | Observation rows |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Training | 1 | 1 | 1 | 3 |
| Test | 201 | 1 | 1 | 3 |

Each subject has one 100 mg dose row. Observation times are 2, 8, and 24 hours in the training snippet and 3, 12, and 48 hours in the test snippet. The files do not demonstrate dropout, population variability, or a representative study design.

The [data dictionary](https://github.com/AIML-SIG/pmx_benchmarks/blob/main/benchmarks/example-pk-model-selection/data/data-dictionary.yml) covers all columns. Dose rows use `.` for a missing dependent variable; readers should treat it as missing.

## Illustrative tasks

These task definitions match `metadata.yml`. They describe what a complete dataset could support; the current snippets are not sufficient for meaningful scores.

| Task | Type | Metric | Output columns |
|---|---|---|---|
| Structural model selection | Classification | Accuracy | `MODEL_SELECTED` |
| Covariate model selection | Classification | F1 | `COVARIATE`, `SELECTED` |
| Concentration prediction | Regression | RMSE | `ID`, `TIME`, `PRED` |

A full submission must specify the candidate models, covariate effects and scoring truth, and exactly how each metric is calculated. For the prediction task, `DV` is the target and only observation rows (`EVID=0`) would be scored.

## Train/test split

The two snippets use different subjects. They illustrate file separation, rather than a validated split strategy. A complete benchmark must explain how subjects or observations were assigned, why the split fits its scientific question, and how test data are reserved for evaluation.

## Read the example files

Retrieve data with Git LFS after cloning the repository: `git lfs install`, then `git lfs pull`. Run the following from this example's directory:

```python
import pandas as pd

train = pd.read_csv('data/train.csv', na_values=['.'])
test = pd.read_csv('data/test.csv', na_values=['.'])
```
